title: Encode, Store, Retrieve
description: Memory's three jobs, how each one fails, and your baseline score
tryIt: Before you sleep tonight, write down as many of the twelve baseline words as you can without looking, and keep that score beside the one from the lesson.

concepts.title: How it works: three jobs, three ways to fail
concepts.contentHtml:
Someone reads you twelve words, once. How many will you still have tomorrow? Before this course hands you a single trick, it helps to know what you are training, because memory is not one thing. It is three jobs, done one after another.

The open textbook Psychology 2e describes memory as the set of processes used to encode, store, and retrieve information over different periods of time.1 Encoding is getting information in. Storage is keeping it. Retrieval is getting it out of memory and back into awareness. Each job can fail on its own, and each failure needs a different fix.

Encoding fails more often than you would guess. In a 2015 study at the University of California, Los Angeles, only 1 participant out of 85 correctly drew the Apple logo from memory,2 and fewer than half could even pick out the real one when shown options. Worse, they felt sure of themselves: confidence ran higher than performance.3 Seeing something every day is not the same as encoding it.

Retrieval comes in three strengths. Recall means getting information out with no cues, as in an essay exam.4 Recognition means identifying something when you meet it again, as in a multiple-choice test or spotting old classmates at a reunion. Relearning is the quiet one: learning something a second time goes faster than the first. In lesson 3 you will meet the man who turned that speed-up into a measuring tool, and in lesson 4 you will see that retrieval is not just a way of checking memory but a way of building it.

concepts.title: Drill: your baseline list
concepts.contentHtml:
Every coach starts with a baseline. Before you learn a single technique, find out what your memory does on its own, so that later you can see exactly what the methods add. Be honest: the score is only for you.

  1. Read each word once, slowly. About three seconds a word, out loud if you can. No going back.
  2. Use no tricks. Do not build a story or a picture on purpose. Just read, the way you would read any list.
  3. Clear your head. Look away and count backwards from 30 in threes,1 a filler task the same textbook uses in its own memory demonstration, so you are not simply holding the last few words in mind.
  4. Write down every word you can, in order if possible.
  5. Score yourself. One point per word, and note how many sit in the right position. Keep both numbers: lesson 5 asks for them.
Drill Your baseline: read these twelve words once, with no technique, then do steps 3 to 5. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. anchor
  2. justice
  3. violin
  4. carpet
  5. rumor
  6. lemon
  7. glacier
  8. honesty
  9. bicycle
  10. method
  11. parrot
  12. theory

How did it feel? You may notice that some words stuck at once while others slid straight off. Make a note of which ones; by lesson 5 you will know why. And keep the list out of sight from now on, because tonight's memory drill asks for it again.

concepts.title: Myth check: the camera in your head
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Memory works like a video camera: everything you see is recorded, and remembering is pressing play.
Reality In a representative telephone survey of 1,500 Americans published in 2011,1 Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris found that 63 percent agreed that memory works like a video camera, accurately recording events so that we can review them later.2 All 16 memory experts they asked disagreed.3 Remembering is closer to rebuilding than to replaying: you keep fragments and meaning, then reconstruct the rest, which is how the Apple logo comes back wrong and how you can be confident and mistaken at the same time.

Wait, really? Retrieval runs on cues, and the most famous demonstration took place in the sea. In 1975 Godden and Baddeley had divers learn lists of words either on land or underwater, and recall of the materials was much better in the same environment.4 It became a textbook classic. Then in 2021 Jaap Murre repeated it with sixteen divers from clubs around Amsterdam and found no advantage for recalling in the place of learning.5 He points to differences between the two studies, including the many distractions the original divers faced in open water near Oban, Scotland, including almost being run over by an ex-army DUKW,6 an amphibious truck.

So treat the place where you learned something as one possible cue, not a law of memory. Better still, build cues you can carry anywhere. That, as you will discover, is exactly what a memory palace is.

title: Seven, or Four?
description: The narrow doorway of short-term memory, Miller's seven, Cowan's four and chunking
tryIt: Ask a friend to read you random digits about one a second, starting with four and adding one each round until you fail twice, then go again grouping them in threes and see how far your span stretches.

concepts.title: How it works: a narrow doorway
concepts.contentHtml:
Read this once, look away and say it back: 7, 3, 9, 1, 4, 8, 2, 6, 5, 0, 3, 7. Twelve digits is well past what most people can hold. Everything you ever memorize has to squeeze through this narrow doorway first, so it pays to know its size.

Hermann Ebbinghaus measured his own in the 1880s. Asking how many nonsense syllables he could recite after only one reading, he answered: "For me the number is usually seven."1 In 1956 George Miller of Harvard pulled the evidence together in a famous paper, "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two". He opened with a joke, "My problem is that I have been persecuted by an integer2", and wrote that for a lot of different kinds of test materials the span of immediate memory is about seven items.3

His deeper point was about what counts as an item. The span is a fixed number of chunks, familiar units, not a fixed amount of information, so you can stretch it by recoding: building larger chunks, each holding more. Miller described Sidney Smith, who recoded strings of binary digits into bigger groups and could then repeat about 40 binary digits without error.4 A beginner in Morse code hears each dit and dah as a separate chunk;5 with practice the sounds become letters, then words, then whole phrases.

The doorway also closes quickly. In a classic 1959 experiment by Peterson and Peterson, people remembered about 80 percent of three-letter strings after 3 seconds but only 10 percent after 18 seconds.6 Later work showed that interference from earlier items explains part of that loss, not just the passing seconds. Short-term memory is a desk, not a warehouse: small, quickly cluttered and constantly cleared.

concepts.title: Drill: find your span, then cheat it
concepts.contentHtml:
Time to measure your own doorway, and then to widen it the way Miller described. For the first part you need a friend, or a random number generator and a voice recorder.

  1. Get your raw span. Have someone read random digits aloud at about one a second, starting with four. Write them down when they stop.
  2. Add one digit each round until you fail two strings of the same length. Your span is the longest string you got right. For most people it lands near 7 plus or minus 2.1
  3. Now chunk. Ask for a fresh long string and group it in threes as you hear it, with a beat of silence in your inner voice between groups: 739, 148, 265.
  4. Give the chunks meaning. A year, a time, a price, a bus route: any group you already know becomes one item instead of three or four.
  5. Try the drill card. Read the letters once, in order, hunting for familiar groups. Then look away and write them out.
Drill Read these twelve letters once, in order, and find the chunks hiding in them. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. N
  2. H
  3. S
  4. B
  5. B
  6. C
  7. D
  8. I
  9. Y
  10. F
  11. B
  12. I

Twelve separate letters would swamp a desk that holds about four things. Four familiar abbreviations fit with room to spare. Nothing about your memory changed in the last minute; only the size of what counts as one item. Hold on to that idea, because every system in this course, from the major system to the memory palace, is a way of making bigger chunks.

concepts.title: Myth check: the magic number
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Your short-term memory holds seven things.
Reality Seven was never a precise law. In 2001 Cowan of the University of Missouri argued that Miller's number was meant more as a rough estimate and a rhetorical device than as a real capacity limit.1 When people are stopped from rehearsing or from grouping items into bigger chunks, the evidence points to a single, central limit of about four chunks, somewhere between three and five.2 Miller himself closed his paper suspecting that all the famous sevens were "a pernicious, Pythagorean coincidence3".
Myth Your span is fixed, so there is nothing to train.
Reality The desk stays the same size, but what you put on it can grow. In 1980 Ericsson, Chase and Faloon reported a man known as SF who, after more than 230 hours of practice in the laboratory, raised his memory span from 7 to 79 digits.4

Wait, really? SF was a long-distance runner, and he recoded strings of digits into running times he already knew.5 That was the whole secret. When the sequences were made of letters instead, his span remained at seven across the full training period.6

The doorway never widened; he learned to carry bigger parcels through it. That is exactly what the rest of this course teaches you to do.

title: The Forgetting Curve
description: Ebbinghaus's nonsense syllables, the savings method, and why forgotten is not gone
tryIt: Count how many read-throughs it takes you to recite the drill's eight syllables perfectly, then relearn them tomorrow and work out your own savings score.

concepts.title: How it works: a man, 2,300 syllables and a stopwatch
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1879 a 29-year-old German began an experiment with only one subject: himself.1 It took seven months of testing, often up to three sessions a day.2 Hermann Ebbinghaus wanted to measure forgetting, and to do it cleanly he needed material that meant nothing at all.

So he made some. He built syllables of one pattern, a vowel sound between two consonants, about 2,300 of them, mixed them up and drew them out by chance to make lists.3 Nonsense syllables had more uniform characteristics than real words,4 whose meanings and associations differ wildly. His basic task was a row of thirteen, studied until he could recite it in order twice in succession.

Then came his masterstroke, the savings method. After a delay he relearned each row and timed it. The work he saved on relearning, as a share of the original work, measured what memory had kept, even when the row was too faint to recall unaided. If relearning takes just as long as the first learning, savings is 0;5 if the row is still perfectly known, savings is 100 percent. In 1879–80 he ran 163 of these double tests,6 relearning after about 20 minutes, 1 hour, 9 hours, 1 day, 2 days, 6 days or 31 days.

The result is the forgetting curve. One hour after learning, half of the original work had to be spent again.7 Then the fall slowed right down: after a day about a third of the work was still saved, after six days about a quarter, and after a month about a fifth.8 Forgetting is fast at first and then very slow, a shape that later replications have confirmed.

concepts.title: Drill: feel what Ebbinghaus felt
concepts.contentHtml:
Nonsense is hard, and that is exactly what makes it a fair test. Here is a row in the Ebbinghaus style: consonant, vowel, consonant, chosen not to be words. You get to feel the edge of your span from lesson 2, this time from the other side.

  1. Read the row aloud at a steady beat, start to finish, every time. Ebbinghaus did not practice hard passages on their own and slot them back in; even with poetry he always read from beginning to end.1
  2. After each reading, look away and recite. Count the readings until you manage one perfect run.
  3. Write the count down. That is your learning score.
  4. Tomorrow, relearn it the same way and count again. Do not peek at the list first.
  5. Work out your savings. First count minus second count, divided by the first, times 100. Eight readings, then five, gives (8 − 5) ÷ 8 = 37.5 percent.
Drill Learn this row of eight nonsense syllables in order, reading it through until you can recite it once without a slip. The quiz will ask for it.
  1. ZUP
  2. KEB
  3. MIV
  4. DOF
  5. HUL
  6. BIK
  7. WOS
  8. FEP

Ebbinghaus could usually recite seven syllables after one reading, but more cost him dearly. For a row five times that long, over 50 repetitions were necessary, requiring an uninterrupted and concentrated effort for fifteen minutes.2 If your eight felt like hard work, you are in distinguished company.

concepts.title: Myth check: forgotten is not gone
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth If you cannot recall something, it has gone.
Reality Savings say otherwise. Even after a month, about a fifth of the original work was still saved, and Ebbinghaus judged that a complete vanishing of the first learning would take an indefinitely long period of time.1 The Psychology 2e textbook gives an everyday case: a woman who studied Spanish at school is surprised how quickly she picks it up again after not speaking it for 13 years.2 That is relearning, and it is why reviewing old material is never wasted.
Myth The forgetting curve shows that you lose most of everything you learn within a day.
Reality The curve describes one man learning meaningless syllables. Ebbinghaus himself tested meaningful material for comparison: stanzas of Byron's Don Juan, 80 syllables each, which needed hardly nine repetitions apiece.3 He credited the extraordinary advantage to meaning, rhythm, rhyme and a common language.4 The famous steep drop is what memory does with material that has no meaning at all, which is why the rest of this course turns everything into meaning.

Wait, really? In 2015 Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros of the University of Amsterdam repeated the experiment, with Dros, then 22, as the only subject. Squeezing it into 75 days rather than seven months, he spent 70 hours learning and relearning rows, and the results are similar to Ebbinghaus' original data.5 They also found that the curve is not completely smooth: it most probably shows a jump upwards starting at the 24-hour point, which some researchers have put down to the effect of sleep.6

title: Space It, Test It
description: Spaced reviews and retrieval practice, and why rereading fools you
tryIt: Write five questions about something you want to keep, answer them from memory now, tomorrow and in three days, and check the answers only after each attempt.

concepts.title: How it works: the two best-tested tricks
concepts.contentHtml:
Two students get the same short passage and a week to remember it. One reads it four times. The other reads it once, then three times closes the book and writes down everything they can. Who remembers more next week? Place your bet now.

Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke of Washington University in St. Louis ran almost exactly that race in 2006, using passages about the Sun and sea otters from a test-preparation book. In their second experiment the study-only group recalled 83 percent of the ideas after five minutes, against 71 percent for the group that studied once and was tested three times. A week later the order flipped: 40 percent for the rereaders, 61 percent for the testers. And the tests came without feedback;1 nobody told the testers what they had missed.

This is the testing effect, also called retrieval practice: pulling information out of memory is itself a powerful way of putting it in. As the authors put it, testing is a powerful means of improving learning, not just assessing it.2

Its partner is the spacing effect, and Ebbinghaus found it first. For relearning a 12-syllable row, 38 repetitions spread over the three preceding days did as much good as 68 repetitions crammed into the day before.3 A suitable distribution of practice over time, he concluded, is decidedly more advantageous than massing it at a single time. A 2006 review led by Cepeda found 839 assessments of distributed practice in 317 experiments,4 and a pattern in them: the best gap between study sessions grows as the time you need to remember grows.5

concepts.title: Drill: a review plan that works
concepts.contentHtml:
Put the two effects together and you get a routine that costs no extra time, only a different order of work. Use it on anything: a language, a speech, the material in this course.

  1. Turn notes into questions. A question forces retrieval; a highlighted line only invites rereading.
  2. Answer before you look. Say or write your answer from memory first, even when you feel unsure.
  3. Then check, and fix mistakes. Roediger and Karpicke's testers gained without feedback, but checking means you do not keep practicing a wrong answer.
  4. Keep testing what you already know. In a 2008 study of foreign-language vocabulary, Karpicke and Roediger found that repeated studying after learning had no effect on delayed recall, while repeated testing produced a large positive effect.1 Retiring a card the first time you get it right throws that away.
  5. Space the next session by the wait ahead. In a 2008 study of more than 1,350 people,2 Cepeda and colleagues found the best gap before a review was about 20 to 40 percent of the time until a test a week away, falling to 5 to 10 percent for a test a year away.3

In practice: for an exam next week, review after one and a half to three days; to keep something for a year, wait two and a half to five weeks before your first review. Both mistakes cost you. As the gap grows, final scores first rise and then slowly fall,4 so a review that comes too soon is wasted on something you still know cold.

concepts.title: Myth check: rereading feels like learning
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Rereading and highlighting are the safest ways to study.
Reality In 2013 Dunlosky and four colleagues reviewed ten popular techniques. Practice testing and distributed practice were rated high utility, because they help learners of different ages and abilities across many kinds of test.1 Highlighting and rereading were rated low: most students report relying on them, yet they do not consistently boost performance.2
Myth If it feels familiar, you know it.
Reality Familiarity flatters. In Roediger and Karpicke's study, repeated studying increased students' confidence in their ability to remember the material,3 even though it left them worst off a week later. In the 2008 vocabulary study, students' predictions of their own performance were uncorrelated with how they actually did.4

Wait, really? Cramming is not a myth: it works, if your test is in five minutes. On the immediate test the rereaders came out on top. The bill arrives later. Over the following week the study-only group forgot 52 percent of what they had recalled at first and the single-test group 28 percent, while the three-test group forgot just 14 percent. If you only ever check yourself straight after studying, rereading will always look like the winner.

title: Deep Processing and Remarkable Memories
description: Levels of processing, a rematch with your baseline, and the truth about photographic memory
tryIt: Pick ten words from whatever you are reading, ask yourself one question about the meaning of each, and an hour later see how many you can recall without looking.

concepts.title: How it works: depth beats repetition
concepts.contentHtml:
Look at the word BREAD. You could notice that it is in capital letters, that it rhymes with "head", or that you could eat it. Three quick glances, three very different memories.

In 1972 Craik and Lockhart proposed the levels of processing idea: the deeper you think about something, the better you remember it.1 In 1975 Fergus Craik and Endel Tulving put it to the test. People answered questions about words that needed processing at one of three levels: the look of the letters, the sound or rhyme of the word, or its meaning. Then came a recall or recognition test nobody had been warned about,2 and words encoded for meaning were better remembered than those encoded visually or acoustically.3 Relating information to yourself helps further, a finding known as the self-reference effect.

What mattered was the kind of thinking, not the effort of repeating. The Psychology 2e textbook draws the same line between two kinds of rehearsal: repeating information over and over, the way children learn the alphabet song, and elaborative rehearsal, linking new information to something you already know,4 such as noticing that a new phone number shares its area code with your uncle's.

The idea has critics as well as fans. Thirty years on, Craik revisited the 1972 article to survey its legacy and answer common criticisms,5 including how "depth" can be measured at all. The practical lesson has survived the argument: meaning is the strongest glue you have, and every technique in this course is a way of adding it.

concepts.title: Drill: go deep, then beat your baseline
concepts.contentHtml:
Time for a rematch. This list mirrors your lesson 1 baseline, word for word in type: a mix of things you can picture and ideas you cannot. This time, think about every word.

  1. Ask a meaning question about each word, and answer it. Would it fit in a shoebox? Is it pleasant or unpleasant? Where would you find one?
  2. Make it about you. When did you last use, see or feel it? Linking a word to yourself adds the self-reference effect.1
  3. Keep the same pace as before, about three seconds a word, so the comparison is fair. Depth, not extra minutes.
  4. Count backwards from 30 in threes, then write down every word you can.
  5. Compare with your baseline. Same scoring as lesson 1: words recalled, and words in the right place.
Drill Read these twelve words once, asking one meaning question about each, then do steps 4 and 5. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. harbor
  2. freedom
  3. trumpet
  4. blanket
  5. gossip
  6. orange
  7. volcano
  8. kindness
  9. kettle
  10. reason
  11. pigeon
  12. habit

Did your score go up? If it did, that is levels of processing at work. One list is a noisy test, though, so do not read too much into a difference of a word or two. Either way you have now used the first tool of the memory palace: turning a bare word into something that means something to you. The next skills add vivid images, and places to put them.

concepts.title: Myth check: photographic memory
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Some people have a photographic memory: one glance at a page and they can read it back later like a photo.
Reality The nearest real thing is eidetic imagery, and it is rare, mostly found in children and unreliable. In a 1964 study of 150 schoolchildren,1 R. N. and R. B. Haber found 12, or 8 percent,2 who could go on "seeing" a picture after it was taken away, and the ability is apparently virtually absent among adults.3 Even true eidetic images are often sketchy, can include details that were never there,4 and usually fade within half a minute to a few minutes.5 In the words of the psychologist Robert Crowder, eidetic imagery shares practically nothing with the popular concept of photographic memory.6
Myth People with exceptional memories never misremember.
Reality In 2006 Parker, Cahill and McGaugh described AJ, a woman who, given any date, could tell you what she was doing and what day of the week it fell on.7 Such highly superior autobiographical memory (HSAM) is real, yet a 2012 study of eleven people with it found them comparable to matched controls on most standard laboratory memory tests.8 In 2013 people with HSAM were equally as likely as controls to report having seen footage of a plane crash when no such footage exists.9

Wait, really? The most famous memory in psychology belonged to the man A. R. Luria called simply S, whose name, Shereshevskii, became known later. Luria studied him for almost thirty years10 and could find no limit to how much he recalled; once, without warning, he asked for a fifty-word list S had learned sixteen years before, and got it.11 S's method? Rich images, placed at familiar stops along a street he walked in his mind.12 He had apparently worked out the method of loci for himself.13 As the psychologist Charles Thompson concludes, memorists like S are unusual in the amount they can remember but not in the processes they use.14 Those processes are what you learn next.
